items.summary: Nearly three decades of Hurricane Hunter data reveal four features that can help a tilted tropical cyclone straighten its circulation and become capable of intensifying. The findings could give forecasters an earlier warning that a seemingly disorganized storm is becoming primed to strengthen.

items.title: This deep-sea enzyme survives heat that destroys most proteins
items.summary: A deep-sea microbe uses an exceptionally heat-resistant enzyme to turn atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia at temperatures that would destroy most proteins.

items.title: Billions in rare earth elements may be hiding in America’s coal ash
items.summary: Scientists are looking to diatoms, sea sponges, and plants for a cleaner way to recover rare earth elements and other valuable minerals hidden inside coal ash, red mud, and mine tailings.

items.title: Subseasonal predictability and Rossby wave dynamics of blocking high during transitional seasons: insights from three successive events in May–June 2023
Genetically engineered crops increase climate resilience of US fields
Scientists just discovered why Arctic sea ice moves so strangely
items.summary: Arctic sea ice may move in unexpected ways because individual ice floes are constantly colliding and transferring energy. Researchers found that this simple process can explain several long-standing mysteries about how quickly the ice moves and spreads.

items.title: Meteorological drivers of extreme swells on the Peruvian coast
Extratropical teleconnections in a multi-model ensemble nudged towards the observed QBO
Irrigation’s climate benefit could equal 363 years of its own emissions
items.summary: U.S. irrigation produces some greenhouse gas emissions, but new research suggests it prevents vastly more by allowing farmers to grow more food on less land.

items.title: Scientists “truly astonished” by discovery that challenges Earth’s origin story
items.summary: A new study suggests Earth formed almost entirely from material in the inner Solar System, challenging the idea that water-rich material from beyond Jupiter played a major role. If correct, Earth’s water may have been present much closer to the young Sun than scientists previously thought.

items.title: New labour and agricultural damages improve climate cost estimates
Scientists stunned as volcano cloud starts destroying methane
items.summary: The Hunga Tonga eruption may have triggered a surprising chemical reaction that destroyed some of the methane released into the atmosphere. Scientists say the discovery could reshape estimates of methane pollution and inspire new methods for slowing near-term global warming.

items.title: A coral reef thought dead for 60 years is teeming with life
items.summary: More than 60 years after surveys suggested a deep coral reef off Benin was probably dead, scientists have found it alive. Cameras revealed healthy-looking coral patches supporting multiple fish species more than 50 meters beneath the surface.

items.title: This German submarine sank in 1917. It’s still leaking TNT
items.summary: A World War I submarine wreck off Denmark is leaking TNT into the surrounding water, seabed, and marine life more than a century after it sank. Scientists warn that thousands of similar wrecks could pose growing environmental risks as they continue to corrode.

items.title: Marine carbon removal at a crossroads
One Mount Etna eruption took weeks. Another happened in hours
items.summary: Mount Etna’s ancient eruptions followed radically different paths, with some magma lingering near the surface for weeks while other magma raced upward from nearly 30 kilometers deep in just hours.

items.title: Back-to-back Arctic storms can double sea ice loss
items.summary: Scientists have found that Arctic cyclones become especially destructive when several strike one after another. These storm clusters cause about twice as much sea ice loss as isolated cyclones, with impacts that persist roughly two and a half times longer.

items.title: Global warming is breaking a 400-year climate link between two oceans
items.summary: The Indian and Pacific oceans have been climatically linked for centuries, but scientists say that connection is now breaking down in an exceptional way.

items.title: Scientists find water was fueling volcanoes 3 billion years ago
items.summary: Ancient rocks from Western Australia suggest water was reaching deep inside Earth more than three billion years ago, long before modern plate tectonics may have fully developed.

items.title: Wasps are disappearing this summer, and scientists are worried
items.summary: Britain’s wasps have become mysteriously scarce this summer, and scientists suspect an unusual combination of temperature swings, heatwaves, and food shortages may be responsible.

items.title: Compound and heterogeneous relationships between climate extremes and global net migration
items.summary: Climate extremes are increasingly disrupting livelihoods and shaping patterns of human mobility. Their longer-term and compounding relationships with migration remain understudied, particularly at the subnational scale.

items.title: Divergence between physical and emotional heat resilience in Chinese cities
Global shifts in mountain wave turbulence within high resolution climate models
Droughts in western Central Europe and associated atmospheric circulation patterns since 1844
DNA solves the mystery of a body found in the Arctic in 1859
items.summary: Scientists have used DNA from living descendants to identify four more members of the doomed Franklin expedition, including Harry Peglar, whose identity had remained uncertain for 166 years.

items.title: Greening masks stability loss in drylands
Where global warming meets urban development
UNESCO warns there’s close to a 100% chance of a Mediterranean tsunami
items.summary: The Mediterranean may seem far removed from the world’s major tsunami zones, but history and modern modeling show that destructive waves can strike the French Riviera with surprisingly little warning.

items.title: Federation Cannot Replace Stewardship: Governing the Calibration Chain in Continental-Scale Observation Networks
items.summary: Federated earth observation systems depend on calibration and validation infrastructure that most governance conversations treat as a technical detail rather than a foundational dependency.

items.title: What Do We Mean by a Climate Mode? Concepts, Assumptions, and Interpretation in Reduced-Order Climate Dynamics
items.summary: The term climate mode is widely used to describe large-scale patterns of climate variability, yet its meaning is rarely defined with precision.

items.title: No longer polar opposites: the Arctic and the Antarctic are converging towards a seasonally dominated sea-ice regime
items.summary: Over the satellite period, Arctic and Antarctic sea ice extent seemed to follow opposite pathways. Arctic sea ice showed a strong and prolonged decrease until 2007 and then stalled in its rate of decline.

items.title: Physiological flexibility in changing climates
Genetically engineered crop adoption support yields and cultivation under climate change
Overview and Forecasting of the Historic Tornado Outbreak in Southern Brazil on 7 November 2025
items.summary: Tornado outbreaks cause some of the most impactful extreme events associated with convective storms. Despite their destructive potential, these phenomena are barely forecasted in Brazil, and only recently have their reports been systematically documented in that country.

items.title: Quantifying atmospheric and land drivers of hot temperature extremes through explainable Artificial Intelligence
Author Correction: Tree species richness relates to long-term forest photosynthesis increase
Antarctica gained a record 695 billion tons of ice. Scientists found the surprising reason
items.summary: East Antarctica gained an astonishing 695 billion tons of ice between 2021 and 2023, temporarily slowing Antarctica’s long-term decline.

items.title: Indonesia’s most dangerous fires are burning underground
items.summary: Indonesia’s dangerous peat fires are surging early in the 2026 fire season as a strengthening El Niño and severe drought dry out wetlands that can burn underground for months.

items.title: Towards understanding the interannual variability of hail in Switzerland
The Need for a New Comprehensive View of the Middle Atmosphere–The Potential of Infrared Limb-Imaging Tomography
items.summary: Earth’s middle atmosphere spans the deep region from the upper troposphere/lower stratosphere at around 10-km altitude to the mesosphere/lower thermosphere at around 100-km altitude. It is being increasingly recognized for its role in driving extreme surface weather and regional climate change.

items.title: Extreme drought now covers 44% of Puerto Rico
items.summary: Puerto Rico’s normally rainy season has instead brought a severe and fast-growing drought. By August 25, three-quarters of the territory was in at least moderate drought, with extreme drought covering 44 percent and some areas receiving less than 20 percent of their usual rainfall.

items.title: Giant Greenland iceberg slams into Joe Island and survives
items.summary: A giant iceberg measuring more than 76 square kilometers broke from Greenland’s Petermann Glacier in August 2026, marking the Arctic’s largest glacier calving event since 2020.

items.title: Plants may be evolving the wrong traits for a warming world
items.summary: Morning glories may be getting caught in an evolutionary tug-of-war between surviving climate change and attracting increasingly scarce pollinators.

items.title: Deep beneath Mars, scientists find a vast hidden magma system
items.summary: Deep beneath Mars, scientists have found evidence of enormous magmatic systems once thought to require Earth-like plate tectonics. Seismic measurements suggest molten rock repeatedly evolved and recycled itself through the Martian crust, potentially across hundreds or thousands of kilometers.

items.title: A life cycle definition of year-round weather regimes in the North Atlantic European region
Decision Calendars for Cold Regions Hydrological Forecasting: Collaboration in the Transboundary Yukon River Basin
items.summary: Supporting decision-making in hydrological forecasting depends on aligning scientific outputs with the practical needs and timelines of operational centers.

items.title: An energetic perspective on the impact of the Atlantic Multidecadal Variability on the West African Monsoon
From ENSO Prediction to Regional Climate Services: The Scientific Evolution of Seasonal Forecasting in Southern Africa within a U.S.–South Africa Collaborative Framework
items.summary: Seasonal climate forecasting in southern Africa has evolved over three decades from statistical rainfall outlooks to an integrated system combining coupled ocean–atmosphere models, statistical recalibration, probabilistic verification, and sector-specific climate services.

items.title: CAPE-k Student Workshop: ARM Mobile Facility Brings the Australian Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics Communities Together for a Week of Open Science
items.summary: The Clouds And Precipitation Experiment at Kennaook (CAPE-k) student workshop leveraged international scientific expertise as students explored data collected using advanced instrumentation during the CAPE-k campaign in Tasmania, Australia from April 2024 to October 2025.

items.title: Earth may have lost the Sun’s protective shield millions of years ago
items.summary: NASA-funded studies suggest Earth’s climate has been influenced by both the Sun’s travels through dense regions of the Milky Way and the violent superflares of its youth.

One of Earth’s driest places was just covered in snow
items.summary: Rare storms covered huge stretches of Chile’s Atacama Desert in snow and dumped extraordinary amounts of rain on one of the driest regions on Earth. The extreme weather shut down observatories, triggered damaging floods and mudflows, and unfolded against the backdrop of a strengthening El Niño.

items.title: Hundreds of hidden earthquakes found at Antarctica’s Doomsday Glacier
items.summary: Hundreds of previously overlooked seismic events have been detected beneath Antarctica, including 245 near the marine edge of the Thwaites Glacier. Many appear to be glacial earthquakes caused when huge icebergs break off, capsize, and collide with the glacier.

items.title: Scientists find a huge hidden ice reservoir beneath Utah’s mountains
items.summary: Beneath the rocky slopes of Mount Timpanogos lies far more ice than anyone walking across the surface might suspect. Researchers used gravity measurements to map the buried glacier in 3D and found it is about 83% ice, with enough frozen water to fill 600 Olympic swimming pools.

items.title: Manhattan-sized ice island breaks off Greenland’s Petermann Glacier
items.summary: A Manhattan-sized ice island has broken away from Greenland’s Petermann Glacier after years of growing fractures weakened its floating ice tongue. Scientists expect two more huge sections could soon detach, potentially removing about 22 percent of the remaining ice tongue.

items.title: Forces deep inside Earth helped Antarctica freeze before the Arctic
items.summary: Scientists may have solved the mystery of why Antarctica froze millions of years before the Arctic. Slow-moving waves deep inside Earth gradually lifted East Antarctica, building mountains and a high plateau where snow and ice could survive even in a much warmer world.

items.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
items.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4.
